findings.title: AdminNeo SQLite: multi_query Incorrect Check of Function Return Value RCE
findings.summary:
### Summary

This vulnerability is a patch bypass that exploits catastrophic backtracking in a regular expression used to filter ATTACH statements in AdminNeo's SQLite functionality. The original vulnerability (CVE-2021-43008) allowed authenticated users to create PHP files through SQLite ATTACH statements, achieving remote code execution. The patch introduced a regex filter to block ATTACH queries, but this filter is vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking.

Originally reported by @zdi-disclosures in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-3582-q6xq-5vf7

### Analysis

**[Source]** sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:47

```php
$query = get_file("sql_file", true, ";");
```

> User uploads a malicious SQL file through the import form. The file content is read into the `$query` variable without any initial sanitization.

**[Transform]** sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:87

```php
// Query parsing loop that extracts individual SQL statements
```

> The uploaded SQL content is processed in a loop that splits it into individual queries. Each query `$query` is extracted for processing.

**[Context]** sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:65

```php
$space = "(?:\\s|/\\*[\s\S]*?\\*/|(?:#|$line_comment)[^\n]*\n?|--\r?\n)";
```

> Definition of the `$space` regex pattern used in the ATTACH filter. The possessive quantifier `*+` combined with SQLite comment patterns (`--`) creates the catastrophic backtracking vulnerability when many comment lines are processed.

**[Transform]** sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:146

```php
if (DIALECT == "sqlite" && preg_match("~^$space*+ATTACH\\b~i", $q, $match)) {
```

> The ATTACH query filter check. When the regex encounters 350,000 SQLite comment lines (`--`), it triggers catastrophic backtracking. The possessive quantifier `*+` causes exponential backtracking, eventually hitting PHP's backtracking limit and causing `preg_match()` to return `false` instead of `0` or `1`, bypassing the security filter.

**[Sink]**

findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: @nx/maven and @nx/gradle have OS command injection via nx.json plugin options
findings.summary:
## Summary

`@nx/maven` and `@nx/gradle` spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from `nx.json` straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any `nx` command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits `nx.json`, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

## Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary `nx` command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write `nx.json` can already run code through the repository's build files (`./mvnw`, `pom.xml`, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where `nx.json` is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

## Affected & Patched Versions

| Package | Vulnerable | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@nx/maven` | `>= 22.0.2, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |
| `@nx/gradle` | `>= 21.0.0, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Workspaces that register neither `@nx/maven` nor `@nx/gradle` in `nx.json` are unaffected — the vulnerable code only runs from those plugins' graph-construction paths, and no other Nx plugin shares this pattern.

## Remediation

Upgrade to **22.7.9** (22.x line) or **23.1.2** (23.x line) or later:

```
nx migrate 23.1.2
```

Upgrade both `nx` and the affected plugin (`@nx/maven` and/or `@nx/gradle`). The plugin's fix depends on code that ships in the `nx` package, so bumping the plugin without a matching `nx` upgrade will not resolve it.

There is no configuration to change — upgrading is the whole fix. If you cannot upgrade yet, only run `nx` commands in repositories you trust, since a malicious `nx.json` can execute code on a

findings.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs
findings.summary:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #13684](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13684) authorizes the caller with the `readLog` verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's `pipeline/runid` label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant `readLog` on `runs` in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar ([@naruto-lgtm]

findings.title: Forge: Regular expression denial of service in PEM decoding (pem.decode)
findings.summary:
### Summary
`pem.decode()`, which every node-forge API that parses PEM input uses, split messages with a regular expression that takes polynomial time on input without a matching END line, and parsed encapsulated headers with regular expressions that take quadratic time on long header lines. A remote attacker can block the Node.js event loop for seconds to minutes with a crafted input of a few tens of kilobytes. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`pem.decode()` in `lib/pem.js` found PEM messages with this regular expression:

    /\s*-----BEGIN ([A-Z0-9- ]+)-----\r?\n?([\x21-\x7e\s]+?(?:\r?\n\r?\n))?([:A-Za-z0-9+\/=\s]+?)-----END \1-----/g

The optional headers group and the body group are adjacent, lazy, and share characters (whitespace and the base64 alphabet), and the match must end with an END line whose label equals the BEGIN label (`\1`). When no such END line follows, the engine tries every split of the text between the two groups, for every label split and at every BEGIN line in the input. The work grows polynomially with the input length (roughly cubic for repeated BEGIN/END lines with mismatched labels, quadratic for a BEGIN line followed by many newlines).

The encapsulated header parsing in the same function had two smaller quadratic cases: trimming each header line with `/\s+$/`, and an unanchored header regex `([\x21-\x7e]+):...` that retries at every position of a long line without a colon. These are reachable when a message does match.

All PEM entry points call `pem.decode()`, including `pki.certificateFromPem()`, `pki.privateKeyFromPem()`, `pki.publicKeyFromPem()`, `pki.certificationRequestFromPem()`, `pki.encryptedPrivateKeyFromPem()`, `pki.decryptRsaPrivateKey()` and `pkcs7.messageFromPem()`.

The fix replaces the message regular expression with a scanner that indexes the END lines once and matches each BEGIN line in linear time, finding the same messages as before. The one difference: a label containing `-----` (`-----BEGIN A-----B-----`) w

findings.title: Forge: AES-GCM authentication bypass via unvalidated tagLength option
findings.summary:
### Summary

The AES-GCM mode in forge.cipher does not validate the tagLength option passed to start(). With a tagLength of 0 or a value that converts to 0 (such as null, false, '' or '0'), the authentication tag is empty, and decipher.finish() returns true for any ciphertext and additional data when the supplied tag is empty or missing. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`modes.gcm.prototype.start()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` stored the `tagLength` option without validation, and `lib/cipher.js` documented it as accepting "0-128". After processing the data, `afterFinish()` truncates the 16-byte tag with `truncate(16 % (tagLength / 8))`. For a `tagLength` that converts to 0, this is `16 % 0 = NaN`, and truncating by `NaN` empties the tag. On decryption, the start-time check that the supplied `tag` has `tagLength / 8` bytes passes for an empty tag, and the final tag comparison compares two empty strings, so `decipher.finish()` returns `true` for any ciphertext and additional data.

NIST SP 800-38D section 5.2.1.2 allows only tag lengths of 128, 120, 112, 104 and 96 bits, plus 64 and 32 bits for certain applications.

The fix validates `tagLength` in `start()`, for both encryption and decryption. A missing, `null` or `undefined` `tagLength` uses the default of 128 bits. Any other value is converted with `Number()` and must be one of 128, 120, 112, 104, 96, 64 or 32; otherwise `start()` throws "Invalid tag length.". Numeric strings such as `'128'` are still accepted. With a validated `tagLength`, an empty tag no longer matches the expected tag length and is rejected.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. `cipher.start()` now throws an error unless `tagLength` is one of the tag lengths allowed by NIST SP 800-38D (128, 120, 112, 104, 96, 64 or 32 bits); a `null` or `undefined` `tagLength` means the default of 128 bits.

### Workarounds
Do not derive `tagLength` from received data. Pass a fixed `tagLength` (or omit it to use the default of 128 bits), and check that t

findings.title: Forge: PKCS#12 MAC forgery and constant-key PBE via zero iteration count
findings.summary:
### Summary

forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1() accepts a PKCS#12 MAC iteration count of zero (or less) from the input, and the PKCS#12 key derivation function then returns a constant key that does not depend on the password or salt. An attacker who does not know the password can modify a PKCS#12/PFX file and compute a MAC that verifies with any password; PKCS#12 PBE-encrypted private keys prepared the same way decrypt with any password. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`p12.pkcs12FromAsn1()` in `lib/pkcs12.js` reads the MAC iteration count (`MacData.iterations`) from the input and passes it to the PKCS#12 key derivation function `pki.pbe.generatePkcs12Key()` in `lib/pbe.js` (also exposed as `forge.pkcs12.generateKey()`) without checking that it is at least 1. The key derivation function (RFC 7292 Appendix B.2) runs its hash loop `iter` times. With an iteration count of 0 (or an empty or negative INTEGER), no hashing is done and the function returns the PKCS#12 diversifier ID byte repeated, for example `0x03` repeated 20 times for an HMAC-SHA1 MAC key. The result does not depend on the password or the salt, so anyone can compute a valid MAC over arbitrary PFX contents.

The same key derivation function is used by `pki.pbe.getCipherForPKCS12PBE()` for the PKCS#12 password-based encryption schemes `pbeWithSHAAnd3-KeyTripleDES-CBC` and `pbewithSHAAnd40BitRC2-CBC`, whose `pkcs-12PbeParams` iteration count is also read from the input. With an iteration count of 0 or less, the encryption key and IV are constants (`0x01` and `0x02` repeated). This is reached from shrouded key bags and encrypted SafeContents in `pkcs12FromAsn1()`, and from `forge.pki.decryptPrivateKeyInfo()` (for example for `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` PEM input).

RFC 7292 defines `MacData` with `iterations INTEGER DEFAULT 1`; an iteration count only makes sense as 1 or more (RFC 8018 uses `INTEGER (1..MAX)` for the same concept). PBES2 (PBKDF2) encrypted content is not affected.

findings.title: Forge: Denial of service in TLS record processing via a record interleaved with a fragmented handshake message
findings.summary:
### Summary

A connection created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `process()` when it receives a record of another content type while waiting for the rest of a handshake message that was split across records. A peer can trigger this with 18 bytes before the handshake, without authentication, which terminates Node.js processes that use the documented socket wiring. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

In `lib/tls.js`, `_readRecord()` handles a record that arrives while a handshake message split across records is incomplete. If the record has any other content type (change_cipher_spec, alert, application_data or heartbeat), forge correctly reports "Invalid fragmented record." through `c.error()` with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert. That fatal error closes and resets the connection, which sets `c.record` to `null`. `_readRecord()` then continues with `c.record.ready = true` and throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'ready')` out of `process()`. The code is unchanged since the first release.

RFC 5246 section 6.2.1 allows a handshake message to be fragmented across records, and RFC 8446 section 5.1 forbids interleaving handshake messages with other record types. Failing the connection with `unexpected_message` is the intended behavior; the bug is the crash after the error.

node-forge reports TLS protocol errors through the `error` callback, so applications do not normally wrap `process()` in `try`/`catch`. When `process()` is called from a Node.js socket `data` handler, as in the documented usage, the exception is uncaught and terminates the process.

The fix returns from `_readRecord()` right after the fatal error. The connection is failed, the alert is sent and the `error` callback is called as before, and `process()` no longer throws.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The connection still fails with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert and the `error` callback, but `process()` no longer throws.

findings.title: Nuxt dev server exposes generated appSecret through Vite file serving
findings.summary:
### Impact

When no `appSecret` is configured (via `NUXT_APP_SECRET`, `NITRO_APP_SECRET` or `runtimeConfig.appSecret`), `nuxt dev` generates a development secret and stores it in `<buildDir>/app-secret` (by default `.nuxt/app-secret`). The build directory is inside the directories that Nuxt passes to Vite's `server.fs.allow`, so the file can be fetched from the dev server:

```bash
curl http://<dev-server>/_nuxt/@fs/<absolute-path-to-project>/.nuxt/app-secret
```

Anyone who can read it can compute every secret derived from it with `deriveSecret()`, including the default password used by `useSession`, and so can forge session cookies accepted by that dev server.

Exploitation requires direct HTTP access to the dev server. `nuxt dev` listens on localhost by default, so this mainly affects dev servers that are exposed to a network (for example with `--host`, a published container port or a tunnel). A malicious website cannot read the file through a developer's browser: Vite's CORS and host checks prevent pages on other origins from reading the response.

Production builds never generate an `appSecret` and are not affected. Dev servers with an explicitly configured `appSecret` do not use the generated file.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/vite-builder` 4.6.3, which `nuxt` 4.6.3 depends on. The dev server now adds `app-secret` to Vite's `server.fs.deny`, keeping Vite's default deny list.

### Workarounds

Set `NUXT_APP_SECRET` in `.env` to a random value of at least 32 characters (for example the output of `openssl rand -base64 32`), or avoid exposing the dev server to untrusted networks.

If a dev server using a generated secret has been reachable by untrusted clients, delete `.nuxt/app-secret` (a new secret is generated on the next `nuxt dev`) or set `NUXT_APP_SECRET`. Either invalidates existing dev sessions.

findings.title: Nuxt: Dot segments in the request path bypass `server/middleware` path checks and server route rules on page routes
findings.summary:
### Summary

Since `4.6.0`, Nuxt resolves `.` and `..` segments in the request path, including percent-encoded forms such as `%2e`, before rendering a page. Nitro's routing, Nitro's route rules and `server/middleware` see the path with those segments still in place. A request for `/%2e/admin` therefore renders the page at `/admin`, while server-side checks keyed on `/admin` do not apply.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass server-side controls that match on the request path of a page route.

`server/middleware` that checks `event.path` (or `event.node.req.url`) is skipped:

```ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (event.path.startsWith('/admin') && !isAuthenticated(event)) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 401 })
  }
})
```

With this middleware, `/admin` returns 401, but `/%2e/admin`, `/.%2e/admin` and `/x/%2e%2e/admin` reach the middleware with `event.path` set to `/./admin`, `/../admin` and `/x/../admin`, and render `app/pages/admin.vue` along with the data it fetches during server rendering.

Server-side `redirect` and `headers` route rules are skipped in the same way, so `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }` does not redirect `/%2e/admin/secret`, and per-route security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` are not sent.

Not affected:

- API handlers in `server/api` and `server/routes`. Nitro's router does not resolve dot segments, so these requests do not reach the handler.
- `appMiddleware` route rules and middleware declared with `definePageMeta`, which are matched against the resolved route.
- Nuxt `3.x` and `4.0.0` to `4.5.x`, which pass the path to the page router unchanged, so these requests 404.

Browsers resolve dot segments before sending a request, so exploitation requires a client that sends the path as written.

### Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.3` and `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.3`. A page request whose path contains `.` or `..` segments now receives a 404 instead of rendering the page the path resolves to, and

findings.title: Nuxt dev server exposes private runtime config through the Nitro dev bundle
findings.summary:
### Summary

With Nitro 2 (the default server engine in Nuxt 3 and Nuxt 4), the Nitro development server bundle written by `nuxt dev` can be fetched through the Vite dev server. Nitro inlines the resolved `runtimeConfig` into that bundle, so private runtime config values that were resolved at build time can be read by anyone with HTTP access to the dev server.

### Impact

`nuxt dev` writes the Nitro development server bundle to `<buildDir>/dev/index.mjs` (by default `.nuxt/dev/index.mjs`). The build directory is inside the directories Nuxt passes to Vite's `server.fs.allow`, so the bundle is served by the dev server:

```bash
curl http://<dev-server>/_nuxt/@fs/<absolute-path-to-project>/.nuxt/dev/index.mjs
```

The response contains every private (non-`public`) runtime config value that was resolved at build time. That includes values set in `nuxt.config`, such as a secret read from `.env`:

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  runtimeConfig: {
    apiSecret: process.env.API_SECRET,
  },
})
```

From Nuxt 4.6.0, it also includes the generated development `appSecret`. Vite's default deny list blocks `.env` itself, but not the bundle containing values read from it.

Exploitation requires direct HTTP access to the dev server. `nuxt dev` listens on localhost by default, so this mainly affects dev servers that are exposed to a network (for example with `--host`, a published container port or a tunnel). As far as we can tell, a malicious website cannot read the file through a developer's browser: Vite's CORS and host checks prevent pages on other origins from reading the response.

Production builds are not affected, because the Vite dev server is not used and the server bundle is not served. Nuxt projects using Nitro 3 do not write the server bundle to disk in development and are not affected. Private runtime config values that are left empty in `nuxt.config` and supplied through `NUXT_*` environment variables are applied when the server starts, are not inlined int

findings.title: follow-redirects: Cross-realm sensitiveHeaders arrays are discarded and custom credentials can follow redirects
findings.summary:
### Summary

follow-redirects 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 validate the documented sensitiveHeaders option with instanceof Array. An array created in another JavaScript realm is silently replaced with an empty list, so a caller-declared custom credential header can be forwarded to an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect destination.

### Details

Affected versions

The sensitiveHeaders option was introduced in 1.16.0. Published 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 both reproduced, giving a tested affected range of 1.16.0 through 1.16.1. The source checkout was pinned at revision 46301256333c90b7faac7aa126effe72ec16d16e; the exact npm 1.16.1 artifact reproduced independently.

Root cause

index.js resets options.sensitiveHeaders when its local isArray() helper returns false. That helper uses value instanceof Array, which depends on realm identity. The same file already uses Array.isArray(options.headers), which correctly recognizes arrays across realms.

Suggested remediation

Use Array.isArray(value) for sensitiveHeaders, then validate and normalize each member as a header-name string. Add same-realm and node:vm cross-realm tests for cross-origin redirects, including the array-form headers representation. Verify that custom sensitive names are removed while unrelated headers remain unchanged.

Duplicate review

The public advisory history contains other sensitive-header findings, including array-form headers and regular-expression handling, but focused repository searches found no report describing cross-realm validation as of 2026-10-25. A private or differently worded report may already exist.

```js

const sensitiveHeaders = vm.runInNewContext(`['X-API-Key']`);
```

findings.title: russh's SSH client is susceptible to unbounded allocations via EXT_INFO packets
findings.summary:
### Summary

**All evidence, reproduction steps, and scripts in the report were verified against a real running instance. Nothing is fabricated or synthetic; every verdict is backed by captured output from an actual deployment.** Concretely, the evidence comes from executing the real russh v0.64.1 client packet parser (`Session::process_packet` handling `handle_ext_info`) in a live client session with attacker-supplied packet bodies in the pre-authentication state; the captured output below is from that real execution.

russh's client stores every extension name it parses out of an `EXT_INFO` packet into a per-session vector and never clears, caps, or deduplicates it (`russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:433`, field declared at `russh/src/session.rs:60`). The packet is accepted without limit in the pre-authentication states, so a server - which is exactly the attacker position for a client library, and remains one even after the client has verified its host key - can send an unbounded sequence of these packets and grow the client's memory for as long as the session lives: 400 packets of about 26 KB each, carrying 3000 extension names apiece, retained 49.1 MiB (about 4.8 times the wire bytes) with the vector reaching 1,200,000 entries, while an equal volume of banner packets retained nothing. Two details make this reachable in practice: russh accepts `EXT_INFO` in its pre-auth states with no budget of any kind (its automatic rekey read-limit only engages after authentication), and russh encodes `EXT_INFO` as its own private message number 7 rather than the 8308 value 82, so the check that might interoperate with a well-behaved peer is inoperative - the malicious server simply speaks number 7. The same growth pattern has been accepted by the project before for other pre-auth allocation sinks; this one is a cross-packet accumulator rather than a single-packet allocation, and none of the published advisories covers it.

## Summary

AdminNeo inserts the database server's version string into a `<script>` tag that carries a valid CSP nonce, without any sanitization. A rogue database server can return a crafted version string that breaks out of the JavaScript context and executes arbitrary code. Because the script tag already has a valid nonce, the browser's Content Security Policy does not block execution. No authentication is required when combined with Login CSRF.

Originally reported in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-h6jr-7pr6-grgj

- Target runs AdminNeo
- Attacker controls a reachable MySQL server (a 80-line Python script)

`admin/core/Admin.php`, lines 1285-1286:

findings.title: AdminNeo: CSRF Token Secret Recoverable from Single Observed Token, Enabling Cross-Site Request Forgery
findings.summary:
### Summary

AdminNeo's CSRF protection uses a BREACH-resistant XOR masking scheme, but the implementation transmits both the XOR mask and the masked value in every token. This allows any observer who sees a single CSRF token (via network sniffing, log files, Referrer header, or XSS) to instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens. Additionally, the underlying session token has only ~20 bits of entropy (`rand(1, 1e6)`), making blind brute-force feasible even without token observation.

Originally reported by @az0mb13 in Adminer: [GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh](https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-33j4-hc95-pggg)

### Details
Token generation in `admin/include/functions.inc.php` lines 1181-1184:

```php
function get_token() {
	$rand = rand(1, 1e6);
	return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) . ":$rand";
}
```

Token verification in lines 1189-1192:

```php
function verify_token() {
	list($token, $rand) = explode(":", $_POST["token"]);
	return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) == $token;
}
```

Session token initialized in `admin/include/auth.inc.php` lines 327 and 385:

```php
$_SESSION["token"] = rand(1, 1e6);
```

**Three distinct weaknesses:**
1. **Instant recovery:** The token format `(rand XOR secret):rand` transmits both operands. Recovery is trivial: `secret = masked_value XOR rand`.
2. **Low entropy**: Only 1,000,000 possible session tokens (~20 bits). Blind brute-force requires at most 1M requests.
3. **Loose comparison**: `verify_token()` uses `==` (loose comparison) instead of `===`, enabling PHP type juggling.

### PoC

**Validated against a live AdminNeo 5.5.0 instance (MySQL 8.0, PHP 8.2).**

**Step 1: Observe a single CSRF token**

Load any authenticated AdminNeo page and extract a token from the HTML source. Tokens appear in hidden form fields:

```html
<input type='hidden' name='token' value='222277:990527'>
```

Token observation vectors: Referrer header leak, shared proxy logs, browser history, limited XSS, network snif

findings.title: NationalSecurityAgency/emissary has an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-35571
findings.summary:
### Summary

The URL validation regex `^(https?:/)?/.*` added to emissary's `NavAction.java` allows protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`) and single-slash scheme variants (`http:/evil.com`) to bypass validation, enabling SSRF and open redirect attacks.

### Affected Package

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Package:** NationalSecurityAgency/emissary
- **Affected versions:** < e2078417464b
- **Patched versions:** >= e2078417464b

### Severity

Medium

### CWE

CWE-918 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

### Details

The fix in `NavAction.java` (line 47) introduces a `VALID_LINK` pattern:

```java
Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")
```

This regex is intended to restrict navigation links to relative paths and HTTP/HTTPS URLs. However, it has multiple bypass vectors.

Protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com/...`): The group `(https?:/)?` is optional, so the pattern reduces to `//.*` when the group is absent. This matches `//evil.com/steal?c=SESSION`, which browsers resolve to the current page's protocol plus the attacker's host.

Single-slash scheme (`http:/evil.com`): The regex group captures `http:/` as a valid match, and browsers normalize `http:/evil.com` to `http://evil.com`, creating an open redirect to the attacker's server.

Protocol-relative to cloud metadata (`//169.254.169.254/...`): This enables SSRF to cloud instance metadata endpoints, which is particularly dangerous in AWS/GCP environments where IAM credentials can be retrieved.

The pre-fix code had no validation at all, accepting any URL. The fix blocks `javascript:`, `ftp:`, and `data:` URIs, but the protocol-relative and single-slash bypasses remain exploitable.

### PoC

```python
"""
CVE-2026-35571 - NationalSecurityAgency/emissary SSRF via NavAction

The fix in commit e2078417464b adds URL scheme validation using:
    Pattern.compile("^(https?:/)?/.*")

This allows protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com) and single-slash variants
(http:/evil.com) to bypass the validation.

Tested against: emissary@0d4dc56

findings.title: joserfc: Unbounded JWE General JSON `recipients` Array Leads to CPU Exhaustion (DoS) via Repeated RSA Private-Key Decryption
findings.summary:
### Summary

`joserfc.jwe.decrypt_json()`, the library's public parser for JWE General JSON Serialization, accepts an attacker-controlled `recipients` array of unbounded length and performs one full private-key decryption operation (`decrypt_cek`) for **every** recipient present in the input, with no cap on recipient count. An unauthenticated network attacker who can send a JWE General JSON document to any endpoint that decrypts it with an RSA key (e.g. RSA-OAEP) can force the victim to perform an arbitrary, attacker-chosen number of RSA private-key decryption operations from a single, relatively small HTTP request. This gives the attacker a highly asymmetric CPU-exhaustion (Denial of Service) primitive: local reproduction shows request size growing linearly with recipient count (~396 bytes/recipient) while server-side CPU time grows in lock-step (near 1:1 ratio between recipient-count growth and decrypt-time growth), and the library's only documented mitigation knob, `verify_all_recipients=False`, does **not** reduce the CPU cost, since the decrypt loop attempts every recipient's `decrypt_cek()` unconditionally before that flag is ever consulted. This is CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption) with CVSS v3.1 Base Score 7.5 (High).

### Details

`joserfc` validates and caps several structural elements of a JWE (protected header size, encrypted key size, IV size, ciphertext size, and auth-tag size) inside `src/joserfc/_rfc7516/registry.py`, but performs **no validation whatsoever on the number of entries in the `recipients` array** of a JWE General JSON Serialization object.

2. `src/joserfc/jwe.py:238` — if `"recipie

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
